    Zeta diversity: species shared by several sites at once

    Source: R/beta-uniqueness.R
    beta_zeta.Rd

    Zeta diversity (Hui and McGeoch 2014) is the mean number of species shared by any i sites. Order 1 is mean richness, order 2 the mean number shared by pairs, and so on, so the decline of zeta with order shows how rare and common species contribute to turnover. The mean for each order is computed exactly from the number of sites occupied by each species, \(\zeta_i = \sum_j \binom{k_j}{i} / \binom{n}{i}\), so no sampling of site combinations is needed.

    The shape of the decline is summarised by fitting an exponential form (log zeta against order) and a power law (log zeta against log order); an exponential decline points to turnover driven by chance (species occupy sites independently), a power law to turnover structured by niche or dispersal differences (Hui and McGeoch 2014). The fits are returned by glance().

    Usage

    beta_zeta(
  data,
  site = site,
  species = species,
  abundance = NULL,
  orders = NULL,
  .by = NULL
)

    Arguments

    data

    A data frame in long format, with one row per record.

    site, species

    <tidy-select> The column holding site identifiers and the column holding species names.

    abundance

    <tidy-select> The column holding counts. If NULL (the default), a column called abundance is used when present, otherwise every row counts as one individual.

    orders

    Orders of zeta to compute. Defaults to 1 to the number of sites, up to a maximum of 10.

    .by

    <tidy-select> Optional grouping columns, kept in the output. Grouped data frames are also respected.

    Value

    A td_zeta tibble with the grouping columns, order, zeta (mean number of shared species), ratio (zeta of this order over the previous one, the retention rate) and zeta_simpson (zeta scaled by the minimum richness of the sites in each combination, from 0 to 1; found by enumerating the combinations, so it is NA when an order has more than 5000 of them). glance() gives one row per group and model with slope, r_squared and aic.

    References

    Hui, C. and McGeoch, M. A. (2014). Zeta diversity as a concept and metric that unifies incidence-based biodiversity patterns. The American Naturalist, 184, 684-694. doi:10.1086/678125

    McGeoch, M. A., Latombe, G., Andrew, N. R., Nakagawa, S., Nipperess, D. A., Roige, M., Marzinelli, E. M., Campbell, A. H., Verges, A., Thomas, T., Steinberg, P. D., Selwood, K. E., Henriksen, M. C. and Hui, C. (2019). Measuring continuous compositional change using decline and decay in zeta diversity. Ecology, 100, e02832. doi:10.1002/ecy.2832

    Examples

    z <- beta_zeta(png_ants, .by = season)
z
#> # A tibble: 10 × 5
#>    season order  zeta  ratio zeta_simpson
#>    <chr>  <int> <dbl>  <dbl>        <dbl>
#>  1 dry        1  11   NA           1     
#>  2 dry        2   1.7  0.155       0.168 
#>  3 dry        3   0.4  0.235       0.0521
#>  4 dry        4   0    0           0     
#>  5 dry        5   0   NA           0     
#>  6 wet        1  16.8 NA           1     
#>  7 wet        2   2.8  0.167       0.183 
#>  8 wet        3   0.7  0.25        0.05  
#>  9 wet        4   0.2  0.286       0.02  
#> 10 wet        5   0    0           0     
glance(z)
#> # A tibble: 4 × 5
#>   season model       slope r_squared   aic
#>   <chr>  <chr>       <dbl>     <dbl> <dbl>
#> 1 dry    exponential -1.66     0.995 0.642
#> 2 dry    power_law   -2.98     0.994 0.950
#> 3 wet    exponential -1.47     0.993 1.52 
#> 4 wet    power_law   -3.14     0.987 4.06
